4. The Language and the Metres

Bhavabhiti, with his limited scope, confines himself to Caua-
seni, and models his style on Sanskrit, so that the speakers of
Prakrit are committed to the absurdity of elaborate style in what
is supposed to be a vernacular. For him doubtless as for late:
poets the production of Prakrit was a mechanical task of tians-
forming Sanskrit according to the rules of Vararuci or other
grammarians.
In metre the Mahdviracarita shows a free use of the Cloka, as
is inevitable in an epic play ; it 1s found 129 times; the Cardila-
vikridita (75), Vasantatilaka (39), Cikhaini (31), and Sragdhasa
(28) are the other chief meties, the Upajati, Mandakranta, and
Malini are not rare, but the Arya (3) and Giti (1) are almost
gone, and there are only sporadic Aupacchandasika, Puspitagra,
Prthvi, Praharsini, Rathoddhata, Vangastha, Calini, and Harmi.
The Uttararaémacartia has the same metres, save the Sragdhara,
a curious omission , it adds the Drutavilambita and Mafijubha-
sini, the occuriences of the Cloka are 89, the Cikharini is second
(30), Vasantatilaka third (26), and Cardilavikridita fouth (25).
The Mdlatimadhava has the same metres as the U¢darardaima-
carita plus the Narkutaka! and a Dandaka of six short syllables
and sixteen amphimacers; here the Vasantatilaka takes first
place (49), Cardiillavikridita (32), Cikharini (21), and Harini (12).
The Malini (21) and Mandakranta (15) take on greater impor-
tance, while the Cloka is negligible (14). The fact that there are
only 8 Aryas teflects the changed character of Bhavabhitu’s
versification from that of Kalidasa.

The Sanskrit and the Prakrits offer no special features of
interest. The latter is mainly in Cauiaseni. but the speeches

2. Murari

Murari tells us that he was the son of Crivardhamanaka of the
Maudgalya Gotra and of Tantumati; he claims to be a Maha-
kavi, and arrogates the style of Bala-Valmiki. His date is
uncertain; he is certainly later than Bhavabhiti since he cites
from the Uttararadmacarita, while we have evidence from the
anthologies that he was reckoned by some as superior to Bhava-
bhiiti, apparently his predecessor. A further suggestion as to
date may be derived from the Kashmirian poet Ratnakara,‘ who
in his Haravijaya makes a clear reference to Murari as a drama-
tist, for the effort of Bhattanatha Svamin to disprove the reference
must be deemed completely unsuccessful. As Ratnakara belongs
torthe middle of the ninth century A.D., this gives us that period
as the latest date for Muia:i. Curiously enough, Professor
Konow,® who accepts the dispioof of the reference to Murari in
Ratnakara, admits that the reference to Mutari in Mafikha’s
Crikanthacarzta® (c. A.D.1135) suggests that he was regarded by
that ‘author as earlier than Rajacekhara, a fact which accords
excellently with his priority to Ratnakara, and is far more im-
portant than the fact that he is not cited by the authors on theory

3. Lhe Anargharighava

Murarigdeclares in the prologue to the solitary drama, the
Anargharaghava, which has come down to us, though quota-
tions show that he wrote other works, that his aim is to please
a public tired of terior, horror, violence, and marvels, by a com-
position elevated, heroic, and marvellous throughout, not merely
at the close. He defends his choice of the banal subject of
Rama; his character adds elevation and charm to the poet’s
work, and it would be folly to lay aside so splendid a theme.
The Anargharaghava, however, does little to justify the poet’s
confidence in his choice of topic The theme, treated already
at length by Bhavabhiti, offered no chance of success save for
a great poet, and Murari was not such a poet save in the esti-
mate of occasional later writers who extol his depth (gambhiraté)
without any shadow of justification.
